title: Project Redline: experimenting with modular application architecture
content: Project Redline is an experimental project where I explore different approaches to application architecture. The goal is not just to build an application, but to test ideas about how code should be structured as a project grows. In this project, I started by organizing the code into independent modules. Each module encapsulates a specific responsibility and can evolve without breaking other parts of the system. Why modular architecture? As projects grow, the biggest challenge is not writing code — it is maintaining it. A modular structure helps isolate responsibilities and reduce hidden dependencies. This project acts as a small laboratory where I can test architectural ideas that could later be reused in larger applications.

title: Building a Symfony authentication starter
content: Starting a new Symfony project often involves repeating the same setup: user entities, authentication, login forms, and security configuration. The idea behind symfony-auth-starter is simple: create a ready-to-use foundation for building secure Symfony applications quickly. Included features: - user authentication - login system - basic security configuration - a structure ready for OAuth or API authentication Symfony provides a powerful security system, but the initial setup can take time. A starter repository helps speed up the process and avoids repeating the same configuration steps across multiple projects. This kind of project is particularly useful when building prototypes or new applications that need authentication from day one.

title: Understanding Symfony's security system
content:
Symfony's security system is built around several core concepts: firewalls, user providers, and authenticators.

A firewall defines which parts of an application require authentication. User providers are responsible for loading user data from a database or another storage system.

Authenticators define how users actually log in — for example using a login form, an API token, or OAuth.

Understanding this architecture is key to building flexible authentication systems.

The goal of symfony-auth-starter is to simplify this configuration and provide a clear starting point that developers can extend depending on their needs.

title: SecureScan: experimenting with application security analysis
content:
SecureScan is a small experimental project focused on application security analysis. The idea is to build a simple tool capable of identifying potential security issues in a codebase.

The early versions focus on basic checks such as:
- insecure configurations
- vulnerable dependencies
- common security mistakes

While this type of tool cannot replace a full security audit, it can act as a first layer of automated checks.

The project is also educational. Building a security tool helps understand how professional scanners detect vulnerabilities and analyze application code.

title: Why building developer tools makes you a better engineer
content:
Developers rely on many tools every day: linters, static analyzers, security scanners, and build systems. But building your own developer tools is one of the best ways to understand how these systems actually work.

SecureScan started as an experiment to explore how automated analysis can detect patterns and potential problems in a codebase.

Even a small tool can provide real value by automating repetitive checks and helping maintain consistent code quality.

More importantly, building developer tools changes the way you think about software engineering. Instead of solving problems only inside an application, you start thinking about how to improve the development workflow itself.

title: Adding fuzzy search and new sections to VraithUI
content: The portfolio now has a fuzzy matching engine powering both the command palette (Ctrl+K) and console Tab completion. Typing 'tls' finds 'theme list', 'prj' matches 'open projects'. The scoring system has six tiers — exact, starts-with, word-boundary, substring, acronym, and fuzzy subsequence. Three new sections joined the family: skills.rs (Rust-themed with cargo build animation and animated progress bars), blog.sh (git log-style posts), and resume.json (syntax-highlighted JSON with collapsible sections). Key technical choices: The fuzzy engine is a pure function utility with zero dependencies — shared by both UI consumers without coupling. The suggestion dropdown uses absolute positioning with bottom:100% to overlay the scroll area without disrupting the console's flex layout.

title: Building a terminal-themed portfolio with Vue 3
content: VraithUI is a Neovim-inspired developer portfolio built entirely with Vue 3 and Tailwind CSS — no component library. The architecture mimics a real code editor: EditorShell.vue manages a CSS Grid layout with named areas: header, explorer sidebar, tabline, main content, console, and statusline. Each section is a Vue component loaded via dynamic <component :is>. The command system: A centralized registry in commands.js defines every command as a regex pattern + metadata. The commandStore handles execution, history, and now fuzzy suggestions. Everything is keyboard-accessible — Ctrl+K for palette, Ctrl+J for console. Theming: 15+ themes defined as CSS custom property sets. The theme store persists to localStorage, supports dark/light toggling, and even has hidden themes unlockable via the Konami code.

title: CRM-FORMA: building a custom CRM with Symfony and Vue.js
content: CRM-FORMA is a custom CRM built for training centers. It centralizes all administrative actions — managing courses, learners, trainers, and schedules in one place. Stack choice: Symfony for the backend provides a robust MVC structure with Doctrine ORM for PostgreSQL. Vue.js on the frontend handles reactive data grids and filtering without full page reloads. Challenges solved: - Complex many-to-many relationships between trainers, courses, and learner cohorts - Role-based access control for admin, trainer, and learner views - Calendar-based scheduling with conflict detection Takeaway: Building a real-world business tool teaches you things side projects don't — data integrity, edge cases in user workflows, and the importance of thinking about state transitions before writing code.

title: PokeBattleTower: consuming APIs with React
content: PokeBattleTower is a React application built around the PokéAPI. It features advanced search with dynamic filters, responsive design with Tailwind CSS, and a battle tower mechanic. API design patterns: The app consumes a REST API with paginated endpoints. I implemented debounced search, request caching, and loading states to handle the API's rate limits gracefully. React vs Vue: Having built projects in both, I can say they solve the same problems differently. React's explicit nature (hooks, manual memoization) gives you more control but more footguns. Vue's magic (auto-tracking, computed) is more productive for UI-heavy work. Tailwind for rapid prototyping: The entire UI was built without writing a single CSS file. Tailwind's utility classes + responsive prefixes made it possible to go from design to deployed in a weekend.
